column4: The matching oath names the same place as وَهَٰذَا الْبَلَدِ الْأَمِينِ, making security the explicit quality of the city in which the addressee is placed.
Abraham asks رَبِّ اجْعَلْ هَٰذَا الْبَلَدَ آمِنًا; the city, its safety, and a prayer for that safety are the direct counterpart to the section's inhabited and protected place.

Abraham asks that the settlement be secure and provisioned, while God's answer extends brief provision even to the unbeliever before fire; this ayah joins the section's city, food, faith, and opposite abode.

Abraham says أَسْكَنْتُ مِن ذُرِّيَّتِي in a barren valley beside the inviolable House and asks that produce reach them, directly joining settlement, sanctuary, and the food that makes dwelling possible.
The Messenger is commanded to worship the Lord of هَٰذِهِ الْبَلْدَةِ الَّذِي حَرَّمَهَا; the addressed person, the city, and its God-given inviolability coincide.

The fear that following guidance will mean being snatched from one's land is answered with حَرَمًا آمِنًا to which every kind of fruit is brought, uniting guidance, protected residence, and provision.
The command فَلْيَعْبُدُوا رَبَّ هَٰذَا الْبَيْتِ matches worship of the Lord who made the city sacred; 106:4 states what His lordship provides there.
The Lord of the House feeds against hunger and grants safety against fear, making explicit the section's claim that the sacred city stands as a fed and protected place; 106:3 identifies the House.
God makes the House مَثَابَةً لِّلنَّاسِ وَأَمْنًا and charges Abraham and Ishmael to prepare it for worshippers, showing a place constituted as both return and security.
وَمَن دَخَلَهُ كَانَ آمِنًا makes entry into the House's precinct an entry into protection, the clearest Quranic realization of a secure lodging.
حَرَمًا آمِنًا is set against people being snatched away all around it, sharpening the section's boundary between protected sanctuary and exposed person.
The Kaaba, sacred month, sacrificial animals, and garlands are all appointed as supports for people, joining sacred place, protected time, and the offering headed there.

At the Sacred Mosque the resident الْعَاكِفُ and the visitor الْبَادِ are made equal, while attempted violation receives punishment; the ayah defines the sanctuary through residence, access, and a protected boundary.
The believers are promised entry into the Sacred Mosque آمِنِينَ, with the pilgrimage rites completed, presenting secure arrival at the sacred destination.
The command waits حَتَّىٰ يَبْلُغَ الْهَدْيُ مَحِلَّهُ, exactly staging the sacrificial animal travelling until it reaches its appointed place.
The unbelievers bar the believers from the Sacred Mosque and hold الْهَدْيَ back from أَن يَبْلُغَ مَحِلَّهُ, showing the section's destination scene through its obstruction.
لَا تُحِلُّوا protects God's rites, sacred month, and الْهَدْيَ, while وَإِذَا حَلَلْتُمْ permits hunting after consecration; one ayah displays the root's opposed sanctuary senses.
The penalty for hunting in consecration is هَدْيًا بَالِغَ الْكَعْبَةِ, another exact scene of an offering defined by reaching the sanctuary.
ثُمَّ مَحِلُّهَا إِلَى الْبَيْتِ الْعَتِيقِ explicitly gives sacrificial animals their appointed destination at the Ancient House.
A hostile outsider who asks protection must be sheltered and then conveyed to مَأْمَنَهُ; this enacts the source dictionary's protected stranger and secure lodging against the unprotected man.
This ayah joins those who emigrated with those who gave shelter and aid, then limits aid where a treaty مِيثَاق stands; migration, refuge, and pact meet in one legal scene.
Those who تَبَوَّءُوا الدَّارَ وَالْإِيمَانَ receive and prefer the emigrants, turning settled residence into protection and provision for newcomers.
For faith unconfused by wrongdoing, لَهُمُ الْأَمْنُ وَهُم مُّهْتَدُونَ brings together the section's named roots of security and guidance as one condition.
فَيَحِلَّ عَلَيْكُمْ غَضَبِي uses the section's named sense of wrath descending and becoming due, and the one upon whom it descends then falls.
A calamity may تَحُلُّ قَرِيبًا مِّن دَارِهِمْ, using the same verb for an affliction alighting near the unbelievers' dwelling.
وَيَحِلُّ عَلَيْهِ عَذَابٌ مُّقِيمٌ makes punishment both something that alights and something that remains, fusing the section's descent and residence senses.
The repeated formula وَيَحِلُّ عَلَيْهِ عَذَابٌ مُّقِيمٌ again presents lasting punishment as an arrival that takes up residence.
The people of Paradise praise the One who أَحَلَّنَا دَارَ الْمُقَامَةِ, the positive endpoint of being placed in an abiding home.
Those who exchange God's favor for unbelief وَأَحَلُّوا قَوْمَهُمْ دَارَ الْبَوَارِ, making leaders place their people in the ruinous opposite of a secure city.
This ayah identifies the preceding دَارَ الْبَوَارِ as Hell and calls it بِئْسَ الْقَرَارُ; its own contribution is the character of that destination as the worst settlement.
God makes houses سَكَنًا and tents light both when travelling and when stopping, directly setting settled home beside departure and temporary encampment.
أَسْكِنُوهُنَّ مِنْ حَيْثُ سَكَنْتُم مِّن وُجْدِكُمْ explicitly ties another person's housing to the resident's means, supporting the section's claim that dwelling depends on provision.
God guarantees every creature's provision and knows مُسْتَقَرَّهَا وَمُسْتَوْدَعَهَا, placing sustenance beside its settled and entrusted locations.
After expulsion from the garden, earth becomes مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ; lost dwelling is answered by a measured new settlement and provision.
The repeated descent scene gives humankind on earth مُسْتَقَرٌّ وَمَتَاعٌ إِلَىٰ حِينٍ, joining relocation, residence, and temporary sustenance.
Had the people of the towns believed, blessings would have opened from heaven and earth; their denial brings seizure instead, making residents' faith determine whether their place is fed or punished.
Saba's dwelling is a sign with gardens, the command to eat God's provision, and بَلْدَةٌ طَيِّبَةٌ, presenting a good town through the sustenance of its inhabitants.
Joseph says ادْخُلُوا مِصْرَ ... آمِنِينَ, staging entry into an inhabited land as arrival into safety.
ادْخُلُوهَا بِسَلَامٍ آمِنِينَ makes the final garden a protected place entered and inhabited, extending the city's security to the lasting abode.
The God-fearing are placed فِي مَقَامٍ أَمِينٍ, a secure station whose provisioned setting is supplied by 44:52.
Gardens and springs furnish the secure station named in 44:51, so this ayah contributes the sustenance and setting of that protected abode.
A treaty made with polytheists عِندَ الْمَسْجِدِ الْحَرَامِ must be honored while they honor it, directly locating pact and mutual protection at the sanctuary.
The offenders broke their oaths and intended إِخْرَاجِ الرَّسُولِ, joining the section's truce sense with the threatened removal of the addressed man from his place.
The unbelievers plot to detain, kill, or expel the Messenger, exposing the man addressed in the city as one denied ordinary protection.
When the unbelievers expel the Messenger, God protects him as one of two in the cave; forced departure from the city becomes a scene of divine refuge.
The addressee is nearly uprooted from the land so as to be expelled, after which his expellers would remain only briefly; residence and removal directly turn on his presence.
The stronger town is called قَرْيَتِكَ الَّتِي أَخْرَجَتْكَ, making the Messenger's own city an agent through its inhabitants' expulsion of him and then subject to destruction.
Oppressed residents ask to be brought out of هَٰذِهِ الْقَرْيَةِ الظَّالِمِ أَهْلُهَا and given a protector and helper, defining a city by inhabitants who have made dwelling unsafe.
Those expelled unjustly from their homes are linked to God's protection of houses of worship from demolition, joining lost residence with the defense of sacred places.
Barring God's path and the Sacred Mosque and expelling its people are named together as grave offenses, making sanctuary include both access and inhabitants' right to remain.
God restrains both sides' hands in the valley of Mecca, creating protected space amid conflict; 48:25 then shows access to the sanctuary and the offering still blocked.
Neither the sacrificial animals' flesh nor blood reaches God, but piety does; this distinguishes the offering's physical arrival at its place from what spiritually reaches God.
Sacrificial camels are God's signs and, once laid down, feed both the contented and the asker, joining the offering at the sanctuary with provision for people in need.
The two sons of Adam each offer قُرْبَانًا and acceptance distinguishes them, directly realizing the source dictionary's thing brought near to God.
قُرْبَانٍ تَأْكُلُهُ النَّارُ names an offering consumed by fire, a direct Quranic scene for the dictionary sense attached to the section's قرب root.
Some spending is taken as قُرُبَاتٍ عِندَ اللَّهِ and a means to the Messenger's prayers, confirming that what brings near can be expenditure rather than an animal offering.
A man comes from the far end of the city to warn Moses that the chiefs plan to kill him and tells him to leave, a parallel city scene of an unprotected man; 28:21 gives the flight.
Moses leaves the city fearful and watchful, asking rescue from its wrongdoing people; 28:20 supplies the urban plot and 28:22 the guided journey that follows.
The emigrant in God's cause is promised many places of refuge and abundance on earth, directly opposing forced departure with new protected and provisioned places.
أَتُتْرَكُونَ فِي مَا هَاهُنَا آمِنِينَ questions whether Thamud can remain secure in place; 26:147-149 spell out the provision and houses meant by 'here.'
Thamud carve houses from the mountains, the resident-made built environment within the secure and provisioned place described in 26:146-148.
Visible settlements are set along Saba's route and they are told to travel among them nights and days آمِنِينَ, combining bounded towns, movement, and security.
A town once secure and tranquil with abundant provision becomes clothed in hunger and fear for ingratitude, the exact reversal of the section's protected and fed city.
The people of towns feel secure while divine might can come by night as they sleep, setting inhabited repose against punishment alighting without warning.
The people of towns feel secure while punishment can come in daylight during play, completing the day-and-night boundary around false urban safety.
The rhetorical question denies that anyone can be secure from God's plan, qualifying every claim of safety attached to a place.
Thamud carve mountain houses آمِنِينَ, a humanly fortified residence whose security is overturned by the cry in 15:83.
The blast takes the secure house-builders at morning, contributing the descending catastrophe that exposes the limit of the safety claimed in 15:82.
After the safe, closely spaced journey of 34:18, the people ask for longer stages and are scattered, reversing connected secure settlements into dispersal.
This near life is temporary enjoyment while the Hereafter is دَارُ الْقَرَارِ, drawing the boundary between a passing station and the lasting home.
Hell is called سَاءَتْ مُسْتَقَرًّا وَمُقَامًا, the evil settled residence that illuminates the opposite endpoint from the secure abiding home.
Towns exulting in their livelihood are destroyed and their dwellings remain almost wholly uninhabited, reversing provisioned residence into an emptied place.
Provision for servants revives بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا; here the named root denotes lifeless land rather than an inhabited city, while sustenance turns it toward habitation.
Fighting is forbidden at the Sacred Mosque until aggression occurs there, and expulsion is answered in kind; the ayah marks the sanctuary's protection and the boundary at which it is violated.
Sea game is permitted while land game is forbidden as long as people remain in consecration, clarifying the legal boundary between حِلّ and حَرَم around the sanctuary journey.
After fleeing the city, Moses hopes his Lord will يَهْدِيَنِي سَوَاءَ السَّبِيلِ; the ayah links displacement to guidance toward a new destination, continuing 28:20-21.
Gardens and springs are part of the 'here' in which Thamud expects to remain secure in 26:146, contributing the provisioned landscape of the settlement.
Fields and soft-clustered palms add cultivated food to the secure settlement of 26:146 before 26:149 names its carved houses.
Treaties with polytheists who have kept every term must be fulfilled to their end, a direct formulation of the source dictionary's truce and of protection bounded by covenant.
If the enemy inclines to peace, the Messenger must incline to it and trust God, giving the truce sense named under the section's oath root a direct Quranic stance.
Each person is ordered to spend according to what God has given, supplying the means-based maintenance principle that continues the housing command in 65:6.
Pilgrims name God over provided livestock, then eat and feed the destitute, linking the journey to the House, sacrificial provision, and the poor person's food.
The command to pray to the Lord and sacrifice gives a compressed speaker stance for the source dictionary's offering brought near to God.
Those who emigrate after being wronged are promised a good lodging in this world, replacing forced movement with a divinely provided place.

Believing servants are told that God's earth is spacious and to worship Him, so an unsafe dwelling need not imprison worship; this parallels worship of the Lord of the sacred city under threatened migration.
Two travellers ask a town's people for food and are refused hospitality, making the moral character of the place visible through how its residents receive unprovided strangers.
The people of Paradise have the better مُسْتَقَرًّا and resting place, a positive counterpart to the ruinous and painful abodes developed by the section.
The inheritors of Paradise settle wherever they wish in its land, presenting the lasting reward as freely chosen residence.
God promises believers good dwellings in gardens of lasting residence, another explicit pairing of faith with a protected enduring home.
Polytheists are barred from approaching the Sacred Mosque, while fear of poverty is answered with promised divine enrichment, joining sanctuary boundary and provision.
Those who bar access to the Sacred Mosque are denied its guardianship; the ayah separates mere control by inhabitants from the piety that warrants protection of the place.
Pack animals carry burdens to a بَلَد that people could scarcely reach unaided, presenting a town as a journey's destination and echoing the offering that walks until its appointed place.
Rain is driven to بَلَدٍ مَّيِّتٍ and brings forth fruit, using the section's city root for lifeless land whose capacity to sustain inhabitants is restored; 7:58 contrasts kinds of land.
الْبَلَدُ الطَّيِّبُ yields vegetation while bad land yields little, making the quality of the place legible in its provision and completing 7:57's revived-land scene.
Water revives بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا and gives drink to animals and many people, linking the different 'dead land' sense of بلد to the section's fed human place.
Clouds are driven to بَلَدٍ مَّيِّتٍ and the earth is revived, a different sense of the city root that marks the boundary between lifeless ground and a place able to host life.
Measured water revives بَلْدَةً مَّيْتًا, making the land's habitability depend on provision that arrives by measure.
Those who follow divine guidance are promised no fear and no grief, pairing the section's guidance root with the security that the city image seeks.
People claim their houses are exposed and seek permission to leave, though the ayah says they only intend flight; it tests the claimed boundary between unsafe home and departure.
God does not destroy towns unjustly while their people are reformers, directly making a settlement's fate answer to the conduct of those who inhabit it.
A town's affluent inhabitants transgress and the sentence falls on the town, joining resident-shaped place with punishment becoming due.
The towns are destroyed when their inhabitants do wrong, with an appointed time for destruction, again locating a place's fate in its residents and a measured arrival.
Destroyed wrongdoing towns leave collapsed roofs, abandoned wells, and lofty palaces, showing the built marks of settlement after inhabitants and protection are gone.
God does not destroy towns until a messenger addresses their central town, and destruction follows only the inhabitants' wrongdoing; speaker and residents define the city's accountability.

The promise to return the addressee to مَعَادٍ can be read as return to Mecca after departure; that place-identification is interpretive, but it specifically answers the image of the Messenger placed in and expelled from the city.
The first House established for humankind is at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for all peoples; it joins the city's sacred center to the section's guidance root.

The bond or accustomed security of Quraysh identifies the resident people whose ordered life belongs to the House; 106:2 specifies the journeys sustaining that life and 106:3-4 its Lord, food, and safety.
The winter and summer caravans show the fed city's residence depending on regular departure and return, a concrete meeting of settlement, travel, and provision completed in 106:3-4.
God assigns Abraham the site of the House and commands him to purify it for worshippers, showing sacred place being prepared through human residence and service; 22:27 brings people to it.
Pilgrims come on foot and lean mounts from every distant pass, a direct arrival scene at the sacred destination whose rites and offerings continue in 22:28-33.
Pilgrims complete their rites, fulfill vows, and circle the Ancient House, locating the vowed act at the destination reached in the surrounding pilgrimage passage.
The ayah commands fulfillment of covenants, makes livestock lawful, and withholds hunting while consecrated; pact, offering-animal, and the root's lawful/sacred boundary converge.
The aggressors respect neither bond nor covenant toward a believer, closely realizing the source dictionary's exposed person who has no عهد or حرمة.
Breaking oaths after covenant makes the offenders leaders of disbelief to be opposed; it directly joins oath and failed truce, and 9:13 adds their attempt to expel the Messenger.
Those who neither fight believers over religion nor expel them from their homes may receive kindness and justice, defining peaceful protection by the absence of expulsion; 60:9 supplies the boundary.
The forbidden allies are precisely those who fight, expel believers from their homes, or assist that expulsion, making loss of dwelling the line that ends peaceful relations in 60:8.
People joined to a treaty community, or those who withdraw and offer peace, are protected from attack; refuge, pact, and restraint from fighting meet explicitly.
Those seeking safety from both sides lose that protection if they neither withdraw nor offer peace, showing the covenant boundary by its failure and continuing 4:90.

In the sanctuary conflict, unbelieving zeal is answered when God sends السَّكِينَةَ upon the Messenger and believers; this nearby ayah gives the dwelling root's tranquility sense to the people blocked in 48:25.
God ransoms Abraham's son with a great sacrifice, a direct sacrificial offering that resolves the submission and intended slaughter of 37:102-103.
The declaration that prayer, sacrifice, life, and death belong to God states the consecrating stance behind the dictionary's offering brought near to Him.
Believers have دَارُ السَّلَامِ with their Lord, who is their protecting ally, uniting secure abode and protection as the positive destination.
God calls to دَارِ السَّلَامِ and guides whom He wills to a straight path, directly joining the secure home to the section's guidance root.
A faction boasts that the mightier will expel the lowlier from the city, while the ayah assigns might to God, the Messenger, and believers; civic power is exposed as a claim over who may remain.
The enemy expelled the Messenger and believers solely for faith, so the ayah joins the addressed man's forced departure with the boundary of protective friendship.
The People of the Book are expelled from their homes after believing their fortresses would protect them, and their own houses are ruined; built security, residence, and removal reverse together.
A covenant forbids shedding one another's blood or expelling one another from homes, directly defining residence as protected by pact; 2:85 records its violation.
The covenant people nevertheless kill and expel a group from their homes, then ransom captives, exposing the contradiction between pact and making residents unprotected.
Those who remain oppressed are asked whether God's earth was spacious enough to emigrate, placing unsafe residence against available departure; 4:98 names those unable to make that move.
Those who emigrate after persecution, then strive and endure, receive divine forgiveness and mercy, making forced displacement a passage into protection.
Those who emigrate and those who shelter and aid them are called true believers and promised forgiveness and generous provision, adding sustenance to the refuge scene stated in 8:72.
The sheltered youths send one companion cautiously into the city to buy wholesome food, joining refuge, urban provision, and the danger of discovery; 18:20 states that danger.
If the city's people discover the youths, they will stone them or force them back into their creed, revealing the provision-bearing city of 18:19 as unsafe for the outsiders.
God makes the earth manageable, commands people to walk its paths, and tells them to eat His provision, joining inhabitable ground, movement, and sustenance.
Adam is warned that the enemy may expel him and his wife from the garden and make him suffer, a direct loss-of-dwelling scene whose material security is detailed in 20:118-119.
The garden's dwelling guarantees neither hunger nor nakedness, making residence inseparable from provision and shelter; 20:117 supplies the threat of expulsion.
The garden also guarantees neither thirst nor exposure to the sun, completing the protected, provisioned home described in 20:117-118.
The blast overtakes the wrongdoers and leaves them lifeless in their homes, another exact meeting of settled houses and punishment arriving; 11:68 describes the erasure of their residence.
Thamud are said to be as though they had never dwelt there, making the inhabitants' disappearance undo the place itself after the blast of 11:67.
Had God not decreed evacuation for them, worldly punishment would have come instead, while fire remains in the Hereafter; this ayah distinguishes exile from the two punitive abodes after 59:2.
The question asks whether people feel secure from the inhabited earth being made to swallow them, placing confidence in one's ground against sudden divine upheaval.
The next question asks whether people feel secure from a stone-bearing storm, extending 67:16's boundary on place-based safety to punishment descending from above.
Many towns receive divine punishment by night or during midday rest, placing catastrophe precisely within the rhythms of inhabited settlement.
The sacred month and sacred things are subject to measured retaliation, defining inviolability through the boundary and proportion of its permitted breach.
Abraham and Ishmael raise the House's foundations and ask acceptance, a concrete instance of inhabitants shaping the sacred place described in 2:125-126.
Honoring God's sacred limits is declared good, while livestock is made lawful except for stated prohibitions; it continues the sanctuary passage through the lawful-inviolable boundary.
Honoring God's sacrificial signs is traced to piety of hearts, supplying the inward protection of the rites whose destination is named in 22:33.
Every community receives a rite for naming God over the livestock He provides, joining offering, divine provision, and worship.
Abraham tells his son of the command to sacrifice him, and the son consents, providing the intended sacrificial act whose ransom appears in 37:107.
Father and son submit and the son is laid down for sacrifice, contributing the bodily placement at the heart of the offering scene resolved in 37:107.
The command to fulfill God's covenant and not break confirmed oaths is a direct Quranic formulation of oath functioning as a protected pact.
Powerless men, women, and children who can neither devise a plan nor find a way are excepted from the migration demand of 4:97, identifying those genuinely trapped in an unsafe place.
Forgiveness is paired with gardens and pleasant dwellings in lasting gardens, repeating the positive endpoint of being placed in an abiding home.
The fire is called the enemies' دَارُ الْخُلْدِ, another ruinous permanent home set against the secure abode.
God establishes humankind on earth and places livelihoods there, expressing the section's link between being made resident and being provisioned.
Believers are lodged in elevated chambers of Paradise, a lasting replacement for insecure earthly residence in the migration passage beginning at 29:56.
Creatures that do not carry their own provision are sustained by God along with people, answering the provision anxiety implicit in leaving one's place in 29:56.
God supplies shade, mountain shelters, and protective clothing, extending the houses and travel tents of 16:80 into the means that make a place habitable and safe.
Night is made for repose and day for seeking God's bounty, connecting the root's rest sense with the alternating provision that supports settled life.
The God-fearing are amid gardens and springs, supplying the provisioned setting into which 15:46 tells them to enter safely.

The elephant episode is traditionally the attempted attack on the Meccan sanctuary; on that contextual identification, the ayah recalls the Lord's protection of the city, though the ayah itself does not name the city or House.
